insight.title: Your Feed Mistakes Your Confusion for Curiosity
insight.subtitle: Lingering on a weird video for three seconds completely rewires your recommendations.

sections.text: You pause on a bizarre video for three seconds just trying to figure out what you're looking at. To you, it’s total bewilderment. To your feed, it’s a ringing endorsement.

Algorithms don't measure joy or approval; they measure dwell time. When you hesitate out of confusion, shock, or mild irritation, the system registers high interest and immediately serves you ten more.
As a result, modern feeds aren’t built from your actual tastes. They are constructed from your micro-pauses, turning weird edge cases and confusing trends into your new digital reality.
You aren't what you like; you're what made you hesitate.

audioBrief.script:
Welcome to your Sift Daily Briefing. Here is the clear, plain version of today's news.

President Donald Trump suggested the United States may launch military action against Iran. He made these remarks ahead of the midterm elections on Tuesday. Trump said the United States still has one or two targets in Iran. He claimed these military strikes could be completed in ten minutes. He also urged Iran to reach a deal. Iran warned that any attack would receive an immediate and unrestricted response. Tehran cautioned that a new conflict could last longer than past engagements. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps reported two tankers caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz. The Iranian military group said the ships hit mines. Diplomatic efforts continue in an attempt to avert further conflict.

Next, financial markets saw a shift between oil prices and bond yields in October. Treasury yields and oil prices had moved together for most of 2026. Jeffrey Rosenberg from BlackRock said this relationship had an eighty percent correlation this year. That pattern stopped last month as artificial intelligence trades declined. Google lost five hundred billion dollars in market value during its largest single-day drop. Rosenberg said investors now view artificial intelligence weakness as broader economic weakness. United States business investment rose twelve point seven percent in the third quarter. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh stated that business spending is broadening beyond tech. Rosenberg warned that persistent inflation still limits the central bank from providing help.

Turning to technology, investors are questioning the large spending on artificial intelligence by major companies. Tech firms continue to invest in expensive computer chips and data centers. Alphabet stock dropped up to thirteen percent after reporting its third-quarter earnings. The company reported nine billion dollars in negative free cash flow. That drop came after fifty-one point four billion dollars in capital spending. To reduce reliance on Nvidia, tech giants are designing their own specialized chips. Alphabet reported over one hundred Google Cloud customers now use its custom chips. These clients include technology firms Apple and Anthropic. The International Monetary Fund said artificial intelligence drove nearly half of recent global trade growth.

In banking news, China's central bank shifted its main policy interest rate to an overnight rate. The People's Bank of China injected five hundred forty-one billion yuan into the banking system. That cash injection equals about eighty-one point three billion dollars at one point two five percent. Analysts said this action lowers borrowing costs for financial institutions by fifteen basis points. The shift follows credit worries tied to the state-owned developer Zhuhai Huafa Group. Regulators scheduled meetings on Monday to discuss tools to support financial markets. Citi analysts noted that broader interest rate cuts are more likely to occur in 2027.

In space exploration, four NASA volunteers finished a simulated Mars mission after three hundred seventy-eight days in isolation. The crew members exited their habitat at the Johnson Space Center in Houston on October thirty-first. The team entered the seventeen-hundred-square-foot habitat in October 2025. During the mission, they grew crops in simulated Martian soil. They also practiced communicating with mission control using realistic space time delays. Medical officer Ellen Ellis said the crew lived in captivity of their own free will. Mission commander Ross Elder said putting humans on Mars is achievable and inevitable. NASA wants to send astronauts to the Moon before attempting a Mars mission in the 2030s. The crew will now spend two weeks undergoing post-mission evaluations with NASA scientists.

Finally, a free trade agreement between Singapore and Argentina took effect on November first. The pact links Singapore with Mercosur, a South American trade bloc founded in 1991. Mercosur represents about two hundred seventy million people across Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay. The agreement was already active between Singapore and the other three member nations. Under the deal, Mercosur will eliminate import tariffs on about ninety-six percent of products. These tariff cuts will take place over up to fifteen years. Around twenty-five percent of product categories received immediate tariff-free access. Singapore's trade ministry said the deal supports efforts to diversify food imports. The agreement also sets rules for logistics, digital trade, and expedited shipping.

Up next, Tesla and Samsung oppose United States tariffs on Vietnam as other firms seek penalties.

Tesla and Samsung oppose proposed new United States trade tariffs on goods from Vietnam. The Trump administration set a November 29 deadline for a trade probe into Vietnam. The government accused Vietnam of failing to protect intellectual property rights. Electric car maker Tesla warned that new tariffs would disrupt its supply chains. Tech company Samsung said Vietnam makes many of its smartphones and network equipment. Samsung is Vietnam's largest foreign investor, having invested about 25 billion dollars there. Industry groups representing steel and software makers supported new penalties instead. The Business Software Alliance said about three-quarters of software in Vietnam was unlicensed. The United States currently charges a 12.5 percent general tariff on Vietnamese goods.

Next, United States sanctions and power outages are causing critical shortages in Cuban hospitals. Cuban officials say only a single oil tanker has reached the island since early January. President Trump tightened sanctions by threatening to punish foreign companies doing business with Cuba. Many foreign companies now refuse to sell medical supplies to Cuban hospitals. At a pediatric hospital in Havana, doctors use root vegetables and chicken for baby formula. Surgeons have used light from their cellphones to finish operations when generators fail. Many doctors have left the country or taken second jobs to survive. Doctors say cancer drugs, anesthetics, and lab equipment remain in critically short supply.

In weather news, intense rainfall caused severe flooding and forced residents to evacuate the Four Corners region. Meteorologists say a super El Niño and a subtropical jet stream caused the heavier rain. They also blame those weather patterns for more torrential storms and bigger floods. Reporter Akiko Fujita is in Huntington Beach, California, while meteorologist Andrew Kozak provides the forecast.

Turning to international politics, Germany's right-wing AfD party is softening its stance on leaving the euro. The party was founded in 2013 to oppose the common European currency. AfD won a regional election in Saxony-Anhalt in September. In October, party co-leader Alice Weidel presented a new strategy paper in Strasbourg. The paper proposes renegotiating treaties for a looser union rather than quitting the euro zone completely. Younger members hope this change helps the party form an alliance with Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Merz's conservative party currently rules out any alliance with the AfD. Weidel declined to say whether she still wants Germany to leave the euro zone eventually.

In business news, American companies are recruiting more women to fill a shortage of skilled trade workers. Federal data shows women made up about 4.4 percent of these workers last year. That figure rose from 2.9 percent a decade earlier. Tower crane operator Sammy Cossairt in Nashville earns 120,000 dollars a year in her role. Construction company Mortenson began offering 12 weeks of paid leave for birth mothers in 2024. More than 10 percent of Mortenson's skilled workforce is now female. Universal Technical Institute says eight percent of its students are now female across 17 campuses. Turner Construction expects revenue of around 35 billion dollars this year as it hires more workers.

Finally, Qatar is leading mediation talks with Iran to prevent new United States military attacks. The mediation efforts took place over the past 72 hours. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said there is still no definitive conclusion to the talks. He mentioned a two-day plan for Iran to stop attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz. President Donald Trump said the United States is not in a hurry to restart attacks. Global oil prices have risen, with Brent crude oil 60 percent higher than before the war. Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned that any new attacks will face an immediate response. It remains unclear whether direct talks between Washington and Tehran will resume.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

Pausing on a bizarre video for just three seconds can completely change your digital recommendations. Algorithms do not measure your joy or approval. Instead, automated systems measure your dwell time on each post. When you hesitate out of confusion or shock, the system registers high interest. It will immediately serve you ten more videos on that topic. This means modern feeds are constructed from micro-pauses rather than your actual tastes. What is interesting is that you are not defined by what you like. Instead, your digital reality is shaped by what made you hesitate. What confused topic made you pause on your feed today?

Thank you for listening to the Sift Daily Briefing today.

audioBriefIndepth.script:
Welcome to your Sift In-Depth Briefing. This full analysis helps you understand the deeper stories behind today's news.

Could a renewed conflict between America and Iran last much longer than past fights? Iran warned that a new war could drag on because the American president cannot dictate its end.

Let us look at how this situation got to this point. On February twenty-eighth, fighting began with US and Israeli strikes on targets in Iran. Tehran retaliated by launching missile and drone attacks across the region. Armed groups aligned with Iran in Lebanon and Yemen joined the combat as well. Iran then claimed control over the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy route. Iran repeatedly targeted ships attempting to cross the strait without its authorization. In response, the United States created a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports. Iran then listed firm conditions before any negotiations could start. Tehran said Washington must unfreeze Iranian assets abroad and end the naval blockade. It also demanded that America lift longstanding sanctions and stop the war on all fronts.

Tensions rose again after President Donald Trump publicly suggested striking remaining sites in Iran.

President Trump said the United States could take care of remaining targets in ten minutes. He specifically named Pickaxe Mountain, which is a suspected underground nuclear complex. Trump also told an Iowa campaign rally he might give Tehran the hammer. News outlet Axios reported Trump held a call with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. A US official called the conversation direct, while an Israeli source called it tough. Sources said Netanyahu pressed Trump to strike Iran immediately after Tuesday's US midterm elections. Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia warned that a new war could last much longer. Akraminia said President Trump would not dictate the timing or conditions of its conclusion. Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebbi echoed a warning from Iran's new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei. Mohebbi said Iran defined a vast theater with no geographical limitations to inflict damage. Meanwhile, Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei said US Vice President JD Vance sent a letter seeking talks. Rezaei noted a positive change in US tone, but said Tehran has not responded. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi stated that Iran remains prepared for both defense and diplomacy.

This military standoff is escalating right now because both America and Israel hold crucial elections.

Anwar Gargash, an Emirati diplomatic adviser, said his country is braced for the worst. Tehran resident Mohadese, a twenty-seven-year-old health inspector, felt helpless about the worrying news. However, forty-eight-year-old vendor Ebrahim said in downtown Tehran that people have been at war for forty-eight years. Listeners should watch whether diplomacy succeeds before the midterm elections end. A renewed conflict could disrupt world energy shipping and push up global gas prices.

Moving from geopolitics to global finance, tech stocks and bond markets are shifting dramatically.

Why did the long-standing link between rising oil prices and government bond yields break down recently? Investors altered their strategy because they viewed artificial intelligence stumbles as a bigger economic threat than oil.

To understand this shift, we need to look at how global financial markets usually trade. A bond is a loan an investor gives to a government or company in exchange for interest. The yield is the annual return an investor gets on that bond. For most of twenty-twenty-six, oil prices and government bond yields moved up together nearly all the time. In fact, they shared an eighty percent correlation over the course of the year. Investors watched oil closely because rising energy costs increase general inflation across the economy. When inflation stays high, the Federal Reserve must keep interest rates elevated to cool off prices. That expectation pushes government bond yields higher as well.

In October, that strong historical pattern between oil and bond yields completely stopped working.

Jeffrey Rosenberg, a portfolio manager at asset manager BlackRock, explained what happened on CNBC's ETF Edge. Rosenberg noted that the market decided geopolitical oil risks are now secondary to artificial intelligence risks. The AI trade suffered a pullback, shown by a Friday Nasdaq wipeout and Google's biggest single-day decline. That drop wiped out half a trillion dollars in market value for Google's parent firm. Investors linked weak tech stocks to broader economic weakness, causing bond yields to fall. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh acknowledged rising oil futures during a recent press conference. However, Warsh argued economic growth is broadening beyond narrow AI pockets into general business spending. He noted that business investment jumped twelve point seven percent in the third quarter. That included a thirty-seven percent rise in information processing equipment. Still, Rosenberg argued that long-term bonds are acting as a safe hedge against disinflationary trends.

This trade broke down this month because artificial intelligence spending is now driving overall economic growth.

Rosenberg warned that bonds are still not a guaranteed safe bet for every investor. Persistent inflation and high energy costs continue to limit how much help the Federal Reserve can offer. Meanwhile, big tech firms like Microsoft are entering the public bond market after nearly a decade away. Rosenberg expects tech giants to issue four trillion dollars in AI debt over four years. Rosenberg suggested trading opportunities in credit default swaps, which measure corporate default risk. Microsoft credit default swap spreads trade near a five-year high of roughly fifty-five. In contrast, Oracle credit default swap spreads trade closer to three hundred. Listeners should watch if rising corporate debt spreads create new risks for the broader stock market.

That heavy borrowing by technology companies connects directly to another growing question for global investors.

Can technology giants afford to keep spending huge sums of money on artificial intelligence infrastructure? Big tech companies continue spending because falling behind in artificial intelligence could destroy their core businesses.

Let us trace how this spending race grew into a global economic force. For years, tech companies have built large data centers filled with advanced computer chips. These chips process the calculations needed to train smart software models. The International Monetary Fund reported that global trade grew eight point three percent between twenty-twenty-three and twenty-twenty-five. However, the IMF noted that trade growth would be near four point six percent without AI products. In Singapore, tech sectors accounted for around seventy-five percent of third-quarter economic growth in twenty-twenty-six. Under a rule known as Scaling Laws, AI models get smarter as computing power increases. Epoch AI estimates available chip compute capacity has grown three point three times per year since twenty-twenty-two. Nvidia designs over sixty percent of these chips. Google and Amazon make up most of the remainder.

Wall Street investors recently began punishing tech companies when heavy spending reduced their cash reserves.

Alphabet, the parent company of Google, saw its stock price drop by up to thirteen percent. That drop erased five hundred billion US dollars in market value after its third-quarter earnings report. Although Alphabet grew revenue by twenty-five percent, it spent fifty-one point four billion dollars on capital expenditures. That spending left the company with nine billion dollars in negative free cash flow. Despite investor anger, cloud companies are building custom chips to lower costs and break Nvidia's hardware monopoly. Alphabet disclosed that over one hundred major Google Cloud customers now use its custom chips. Meanwhile, Japanese investment bank Nomura sees a seventy-five percent chance that the AI spending race will continue. Nomura researcher Changwon Chung called this competition a game of chicken that nobody can quit.

Tech titans refuse to slow down right now because agentic AI tools require even more computing power.

Morgan Stanley economists expect AI capital spending to be higher in twenty-twenty-seven than in twenty-twenty-six. This continued build-out benefits Asian chip-exporting nations that produce essential mature-node power management chips. However, analysts warn that big tech will likely fail to satisfy Wall Street profitability targets for several quarters. That friction could spark further sell-offs in technology stocks.

Up next, China lowers funding costs with a shift to its overnight policy rate.

Why is China changing the way it lends money to its banks? The central bank shifted its main policy rate to lower borrowing costs for financial institutions.

China's economy relies on banks to lend money to businesses and home buyers. To control money flow, China's central bank sets official interest rates. These rates tell commercial banks how much it costs to borrow money short-term. For years, the central bank used a seven-day lending rate as its main tool. Banks borrowed money for seven days, so they paid interest based on that seven-day benchmark rate. When businesses needed cheaper loans, the central bank lowered this seven-day rate to encourage lending. However, seven days can be too long when banks need cash fast to manage daily operations. When money moves slowly through banks, businesses struggle to get quick loans for growth. So, policymakers wanted a faster way to pass cheaper money directly down to financial institutions. Last month, the central bank announced it was considering switching its main benchmark to an overnight rate. An overnight rate lets banks borrow money for just one day at a time. This setup helps cash move faster through the financial system and supports broader economic growth.

The central bank officially made the switch and put the new policy into action on Monday. It began conducting these one-day cash injections every single day instead of using older weekly schedules.

The People's Bank of China injected 541 billion yuan, or 81 point 3 billion US dollars. It provided this cash through overnight reverse repurchase agreements at 1 point 25 percent. Chief economist Ming Ming at CITIC Securities said the policy rate has officially shifted its anchor. Analysts said the move lowers the floor of China's interest rate framework by 15 basis points. Strategic analyst Zhaopeng Xing at ANZ called it a targeted rate cut for financial institutions. He said it boosts their net interest margins by about 5 basis points to support bank profits. However, he noted the move is unlikely to have a material impact on the stock market. Also on Monday, regulators planned meetings with financial institutions to discuss tools for supporting capital markets.

Policymakers faced fresh pressure after credit concerns from state-owned developer Zhuhai Huafa Group unsettled the bond market. These credit troubles worried investors, so officials acted to stabilize confidence and lower costs quickly.

This change could keep cash flowing smoothly, which helps banks absorb financial risks. Yet, analysts at Citi cautioned that this is a market adjustment rather than a true rate cut. Citi analysts do not expect a benchmark Loan Prime Rate cut to follow in November. Instead, Citi sees 2027 as the more likely window for conventional rate cuts. Listeners should watch whether China takes more steps next year to help local debt resolution efforts.

From financial shifts in China, we move to a story about long-distance space travel.

What is it like to spend more than a year locked in a fake Mars habitat? Four crew members just completed 378 days inside a simulated space base to help prepare for Mars.

Humans have long dreamed of sending people to explore the planet Mars. NASA has already sent robotic rovers and orbiting spacecraft to gather pictures and soil data. However, sending living humans across millions of miles presents far bigger physical and mental challenges. Astronauts on Mars would live in cramped spaces without fresh air or fresh food from Earth. They would also experience long communication delays when trying to speak with mission control back home. To prepare, NASA planned human missions to Mars for as early as the 2030s. Before that, NASA plans to send astronauts back to the Moon for the first time since 1972. To test how humans handle isolation, NASA created simulated space missions right here on Earth. They built a special 1,700 square foot 3D-printed habitat at Johnson Space Center in Houston. This program is called the Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog, or CHAPEA. NASA conducted its first CHAPEA mission with four people between 2023 and 2024.

The second four-person crew completed their long stay and stepped outside on October 31. They had entered the closed habitat over a year earlier on October 19, 2025.

The crew included commander Ross Elder and medical officer Ellen Ellis. It also included science officer Matthew Montgomery and flight engineer James Spicer. During their 378 days, they grew crops in simulated Martian soil and lived with strictly limited resources. They also managed habitat maintenance and coped with realistic time delays on all communications with Earth. Center director Vanessa Wyche greeted the returning crew when they stepped out of isolation. She said communication lag times require patience, careful planning, and greater independence from future astronauts. Medical officer Ellen Ellis described the year as living in captivity of their own free will. Mission commander Ross Elder said putting humans on Mars is not only achievable, but rather inevitable. Now, the four crew members face two weeks of post-mission evaluations and debriefings with NASA scientists.

NASA needs data on how daily isolation affects human health, productivity, and connections over long periods. Additionally, Ellis noted a narrowing window of opportunity to maintain United States pre-eminence in space.

Lessons from this mission will help scientists design safer habitats and routines for deep space travel. These insights could pave the way for upcoming lunar missions and an eventual trip to Mars. Listeners can watch for NASA to evaluate this data before launching its third CHAPEA simulation.

From space exploration in Texas, we turn to a new trade agreement across the Pacific Ocean.

How is Singapore building stronger economic links with South America? A landmark free trade pact recently went into effect between Singapore and Argentina.

Singapore is a small island nation that imports most of its food and goods. To keep its economy growing, Singapore relies on open trade with partners around the world. In South America, four countries formed a trade alliance called Mercosur in 1991. Those founding members are Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay. Together, Mercosur represents a total population of about 270 million people. Singapore wanted to connect its businesses with South American markets and secure reliable food supplies. So, Singapore worked to create the Mercosur-Singapore Free Trade Agreement. This agreement already entered into force between Singapore and the other three founding members. Singapore also expanded South American ties through the Pacific Alliance-Singapore Free Trade Agreement in 2025. However, the deal with Mercosur was not complete until Argentina ratified the agreement locally.

On November 1, the trade agreement officially entered into force between Singapore and Argentina. This step completed the rollout of the trade deal across all founding Mercosur nations.

Singapore's Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry announced the news with the Argentinian embassy. They called the entry into force a significant milestone in Singapore's engagement with South America. Under the deal, Mercosur will eliminate import tariffs on about 96 percent of products. This tariff elimination will occur over a period of up to 15 years. Around 25 percent of tariff lines will enjoy tariff-free access right away. The agreement also sets common rules of origin and creates more transparent customs procedures. It speeds up clearance for express shipments and perishable goods. Beyond goods, the deal supports service providers, investors, entrepreneurship, cybersecurity, and small businesses.

Argentina is a major food producer, helping Singapore diversify food sources and strengthen food resilience. In return, Argentine firms can use Singapore's regional hub status to reach South-east Asia.

This deal could boost trade in sectors like energy, infrastructure, logistics, technology, and services. Lower tariffs may help businesses in both regions cut costs and expand faster. Listeners can watch whether trade volumes between Singapore and South America grow in coming years.

Next, we look at why Tesla and Samsung oppose US tariffs on Vietnam while solar firms seek penalties.

Should the United States put new trade taxes on goods coming from Vietnam? Big companies are divided over whether Washington should add these penalties.

Years ago, many global businesses built large factories inside Vietnam. A tariff is a tax that a country places on imported goods. Companies wanted to make products in Vietnam to avoid trade fights between America and China. Over time, Vietnam shipped far more goods to American buyers every year. But trade tensions began to grow between Washington and Vietnam as well. American officials accused Vietnam of failing to protect intellectual property. Intellectual property means legal protection for inventions, software, and creative ideas. In July, Washington placed a twelve point five percent tax on Vietnamese goods. That tax followed an official investigation into forced labor concerns. Earlier, the Supreme Court struck down twenty percent tariffs on imports from Vietnam. Economists say American officials now want to reimpose taxes at least that high. Vietnam has urged Washington to conduct its trade investigations in an objective way. Officials are also running a separate probe into alleged excessive factory capacity in Vietnam.

In May, the United States government launched a broad trade investigation. Officials placed Vietnam on a serious foreign watchlist for trade violations. It was the first country put on that watchlist in thirteen years. Washington set a deadline of November twenty-ninth to finish the inquiry.

Electric car maker Tesla asked officials to consider American manufacturing supply needs. Tesla submitted comments on July second saying certain advanced components cannot be sourced domestically. Tech firm Samsung made a similar argument to the government. Samsung is the largest foreign investor in Vietnam, spending about twenty-five billion dollars there. Vietnam produces many Samsung smartphones and network devices for the American market. Trade groups for footwear, apparel, bikes, and video games also opposed new tariffs. However, groups representing American steel, solar panels, seafood, and wood urged strong penalties. The Business Software Alliance, representing Microsoft, Oracle, and IBM, complained about illegal software. It cited a twenty-seventeen survey showing three-quarters of software on Vietnamese computers was unlicensed. The Motion Picture Association said piracy websites in Vietnam received over twelve point five billion visits last year.

Vietnam's exports to America surged forty-two percent in the first eight months of this year. That jump gave Vietnam the largest goods trade surplus with America. It moved Vietnam ahead of China and Mexico. Washington is facing pressure to act before the November twenty-ninth deadline.

New tariffs could make smartphones, cars, and clothes more expensive for consumers. Supply chains for big tech companies might face disruptions. On the other hand, domestic solar and steel producers could gain protection from foreign competitors. Policymakers must decide whether to punish trade violations or protect company supply lines. Watch for an official ruling from Washington before the end of the month.

Now let's turn to another trade conflict, where strict economic pressures are hitting healthcare on an island nation.

Why are Cuban hospitals running out of basic medicines and reliable electricity? Tough trade rules from the United States have combined with deep economic problems on the island nation.

Cuba sits just ninety miles off the coast of the United States. Communist leader Fidel Castro took control of Cuba in nineteen-fifty-nine. Since the nineteen-sixties, Cuba has been under communist rule. The government controls most businesses, schools, and healthcare facilities. Opposition political parties are illegal under Cuban law. Decades ago, Washington put a trade embargo on Cuba. An embargo is an official law that stops trade with a specific country. Washington blames Cuba's crisis on government corruption and long-term economic mismanagement. Cuban officials say American policies aim to destroy their nation. For decades, Cuba depended on foreign allies for aid. First, the Soviet Union provided heavy financial support. Later, Venezuela sent cheap oil to power Cuba's electrical grid.

On January third, twenty-twenty-six, the United States captured Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro. As a result, Cuba lost its main oil supplier. Cuban officials say only a single oil tanker has arrived since early January. That oil shortage crippled Cuba's electricity system and caused widespread blackouts.

At William Soler Pediatric Hospital in Havana, doctors treated a dehydrated two-month-old baby. ICU chief Dr. Alejandro Chong said the baby weighed under five pounds. Due to supply shortages, doctors fed the baby formula made from malanga root and chicken. Malanga is a starchy root vegetable. Hospital power outages force doctors to use cellphone lights during operations. Chong works at his own food stand because it pays more than running the ICU. Resident doctor Lórien Rodríguez works as a radio announcer to support herself. Patient Paloma Blanco is eight months pregnant and asked friends in America for surgical supplies. Deputy foreign minister Carlos Fernández de Cossío acknowledged government decisions could have been better. But Cossío said foreign pressure heavily harms the Cuban population. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the failing Cuban regime hides billions overseas. Rubio's spokesman added that Cuba blames others for its own corruption. Last week, American ambassador Mike Waltz gave a speech at the United Nations. Cuban diplomats confronted him, and the United States expelled one Cuban diplomat.

President Trump recently increased sanctions against businesses working with Cuba. Foreign suppliers often refuse to sell medical goods to Cuba out of fear of US fines. Stalled negotiations have left hospitals with critically short supplies of cancer drugs and equipment.

Cuba made historic economic reforms this year, ending government monopolies on fuel, banking, and pharmacies. American companies now export fuel to private Cuban buyers, but prices are extremely high. Basic foods like eggs can now cost more than a full month of salary. Watch to see if trade tensions ease or if healthcare shortages cause more doctors to leave.

Now for a quick update on extreme weather in the American Southwest.

Intense rainfall caused severe flooding in the Four Corners region, forcing residents across the Southwest to evacuate. Meteorologists say a super El Niño and a subtropical jet stream caused heavier rain, torrential storms, and bigger floods. Akiko Fujita is in Huntington Beach, California with details, while Andrew Kozak provides the forecast in studio.

Next up, as Europe's right advances, Germany's AfD rethinks its anti-euro roots.

Why is Germany's top right-wing political party changing its mind about dropping the euro currency? The party is trying to look like a responsible partner so it can win power.

Let us look back at how this story started. In 2013, several European countries struggled with heavy debts. Other nations in the region agreed to help pay off those debts. Many Germans felt angry about using their tax money for these bailouts. So political leaders formed a new party called Alternative for Germany, or AfD. They wanted Germany to quit using the euro currency. Over time, the party shifted its focus toward opposing immigration. Opponents and domestic intelligence agencies said this line strayed close to dangerous extremism. The party rejected allegations of extremism and kept building support.

Things changed when the party achieved a historic victory in Saxony-Anhalt in September. Surveys now show it is the most popular party nationwide. This success brings the party closer to entering national government before the decade ends.

In October, party co-leader Alice Weidel presented a strategy paper in Strasbourg. She stood alongside allies in the Europe of Sovereign Nations group. The paper shifts focus away from quitting the euro or leaving the European Union. It proposes renegotiating treaties to create a looser union instead. Countries could opt out of common policies on defense spending or immigration. Younger members like Jean-Pascal Hohm say hardline views complicate partnerships with conservative parties. Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative party currently rules out any alliance with them.

The party is rethinking its views now because right-wing allies abroad are gaining real power. Lawmaker Sebastian Muenzenmaier says prospects for reforming the union have never been better.

What does this mean for the future? Political science professor Wolfgang Schroeder argues that Germany's export economy depends on the global market. He warns that leaving the union could risk the collapse of the national economy. Inside the party, the euro issue remains unsettled. A recent youth resolution on Europe was withdrawn after failing to gain enough support. We should watch whether the party completely drops its anti-euro position in coming years.

While political leaders adjust their visions for Europe, companies across the ocean are making changes of their own.

Why are building and repair companies spending extra effort to hire female workers? Firms need more skilled labor, so they are improving workplace culture to attract women.

Let us look at how the trade industry got to this point. For decades, skilled trades like plumbing, welding, and construction were mostly run by men. Society often viewed trade jobs as heavy physical labor in dirty working conditions. Many young women were encouraged to pursue four-year college degrees instead. Because of these traditions, very few women entered the trade workforce. Federal data showed women made up only two point nine percent of trade workers a decade ago. Over time, construction and repair industries began facing a big shortage of trained workers. Meanwhile, new technology changed the nature of trade work. Automotive technicians started using computers to diagnose complex car problems.

What changed is that companies realized women could fill these open jobs. Today, female participation in the trades has risen to about four point four percent. At Universal Technical Institute, eight percent of students are female. That figure is four times higher than it was five years ago. In collision repair programs, nineteen percent of students are women. Construction firm Mortenson now offers twelve weeks of paid maternity leave. Over ten percent of Mortenson's skilled workforce is now female, up from seven percent a decade ago. Turner Construction expects thirty-five billion dollars in revenue this year, up from twenty-nine billion last year. To keep workers, Turner provides cleaner breakrooms and acts within four hours on harassment reports. Company president Abrar Sheriff says they simply need more people in the industry.

This push is happening now because booming work on data centers has created huge demand for labor.

What does this mean for workers? These jobs pay well without requiring a four-year college degree. Tower crane operator Sammy Cossairt makes one hundred twenty thousand dollars a year. Tile foreman Rebecca Heustess earns sixty-five thousand dollars a year. Mortenson executive Maja Ericksen points out that trade careers are largely safe from artificial intelligence. We should watch whether more states pass laws requiring clean water and nursing rooms on jobsites.

While American companies work to build up their workforce, nations in the Middle East face severe instability.

Why is Qatar rushing to mediate talks between Iran and the United States right now? Qatar hopes to prevent new military strikes that could disrupt the entire region.

Let us look back at how this war began. Eight months ago, a major war broke out involving the United States, Israel, and Iran. Attacks killed Iran's supreme leader and top military commanders. Forces destroyed many Iranian ships and missile production sites. On the first day of fighting, Iran retaliated against American military bases. In Bahrain, Iranian strikes damaged warehouses and radar equipment at a U.S. Navy hub. Base personnel fell from eight thousand workers down to under one hundred. Despite eight months of strikes and economic sanctions, Iran's government remains in power.

Tensions changed sharply over seventy-two hours as leaders braced for potential new attacks following Tuesday's elections. Qatar launched intense mediation efforts to stop a new round of strikes. Qatari mediators visited Tehran, and Iranian delegates traveled to Doha. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi reported no final agreement yet. However, Araghchi mentioned a proposed two-day plan. Iran would stop attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz during direct talks with Washington. President Donald Trump said the United States is not in that much of a hurry. Trump added that most nuclear and military sites are already knocked out. Meanwhile, Iran's new supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei ordered immediate responses to any future threats.

This urgency is happening now because officials fear new strikes could launch right after Tuesday's midterm elections.

What does this conflict mean for the rest of the world? The war has already hit energy markets very hard. Brent crude oil prices are sixty percent higher today than before the war started. Bahrain's Foreign Minister Abdullatif Al Zayani warned that Iran threatened vital undersea internet cables. Emirati diplomat Anwar Gargash stressed that military options will only complicate the situation. We should watch whether Qatar can successfully guide both sides back to direct diplomacy.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

Have you ever paused on a strange video online just to figure out what was happening? You might stand there feeling total bewilderment for just three seconds. To you, that pause is just confusion. To your social media feed, that pause is a ringing endorsement. Computer algorithms do not measure your joy or your approval. Instead, they measure your dwell time, which means how long you stay on a post. When you hesitate because of shock, confusion, or mild irritation, the system takes notice. It registers high interest and immediately sends you ten more videos just like it. This process completely changes what shows up on your screen. Modern feeds are not built from your actual tastes or things you truly enjoy. They are constructed from your tiny micro-pauses. This turns strange edge cases and confusing trends into your new digital reality. It is a fascinating shift in how technology understands human behavior. We like to think our feeds reflect our personality and choices. In reality, you are not what you like. You are what made you hesitate. Next time you linger on a weird post, ask yourself one simple question. Are you showing true interest, or did you just pause out of confusion?

Thank you for listening to Sift In-Depth. We hope you carry these ideas with you as you explore the world.
